prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling frequency measurement at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: I have moved from B019 to B048 as my preferred configuration. The lattice clock rests on one identifiable idea, the magic-wavelength condition that removes the trapping light shift so that many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once. That idea was demonstrated by Katori and carried by Ye to uncertainties near 1e-18. Several independent laboratories have reproduced the result, and it already feeds clock comparisons, relativistic geodesy, tests of varying constants and the preparation of a new SI second. I raised the overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes in round 1, but Kroll and Danielsson argue convincingly that the concept is different: many atoms cancelling the trapping Stark shift, not a new spectroscopy tool or single-ion control. That moves the overlap from an obstacle to a drafting task. Two names fit the concept-and-realisation versus record-accuracy-and-many-body split better than any three-person set I can draw for topological insulators. As a theorist of electronic structure I still rate B019 higher on conceptual novelty, but the prize rewards a defensible, complete credit as well, and B048 offers that more clearly today.
statement.case_against: Two names leave out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the Paris and PTB groups, and the boundary with Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) has to be drawn by the citation wording. My comparison with B019 is unchanged on conceptual novelty: a new classification of phases is a larger shift than a better clock. The redefinition of the second is also still pending, so part of the payoff is anticipated, not realised. Support for B048 is broad because it is nobody's strongly contested option, and I do not treat that as a measure of scientific rank. My priority statements for the lattice clock rest on recollection and not on verified records.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is a different concept from the comb and single-ion prizes, because many atoms cancel the trapping Stark shift, and that the Katori and Ye credit maps onto concept and record-setting realisation.
responses.response: In round 1 I called the clock a refinement of a tradition honoured twice. Your exchange with Danielsson changed that. The magic-wavelength condition is a specific physical insight that makes many-atom interrogation possible, and it is not something the comb or ion-control work contains. The chair asks whether the overlap is a real obstacle. I now say no, provided the citation names the lattice clock and not optical clocks in general. I would ask you to confirm that the 1e-18 clause survives scrutiny from the clock community.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the demonstrated impact of the lattice clock already outweighs the timing argument for waiting for the redefinition of the second, and that a two-name credit is clean.
responses.response: I accept this. The redefinition is a consequence of the maturity, not a condition for it, since reproduction at the 1e-18 level across JILA, Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE is already in the record. Waiting would not add scientific evidence and would only delay recognition. I also agree with your caution that Katori's proposal and Ye's later work are different contributions, and that a citation naming both the invention and the development covers each. What I cannot judge is how the comparison figures are best stated, and I rely on you for that.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B048 because its credit is cleaner than B019, where the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal and the 2016 topology prize complicate an equitable trio, while keeping B019 as the strongest alternative.
responses.response: My own answer to you in round 1 was that a citation limited to the Z2 prediction and the first observation of the quantum spin Hall state could be defended. I still think so as a matter of wording, but wording does not change who is absent. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang chose HgTe, and Molenkamp's experiment followed from that, so a visible dispute would travel with the prize. The 2016 prize is a distinct recognition, but it does reduce how urgent a further topology award is. For these reasons I now place B019 second, as the strongest fallback, behind B048.

responses.point: Olsson keeps spherical-aberration correction first as an invention that changed what can be measured, and says B048 would be a defensible outcome, not a poor one.
responses.response: I agree that B028 is a real invention with identifiable inventors, and I accepted in round 1 that the correction question for Krivanek and STEM complicates it. Where we differ is that I weigh the physical reach of a new precision regime tied to fundamental constants above an instrument whose largest impact is in materials science and chemistry. I would not oppose B028 in a later year. This year the broad agreement across the committee on B048, which you accept as defensible, seems to me to be backed by the science and not only by convenience.

responses.point: Johansson ranks trapped-ion quantum logic second and treats it as a serious alternative, with B019 only as a fallback.
responses.response: I keep B003 as my second alternative, partly because of your argument. The Cirac and Zoller proposal and Blatt's demonstrations are a strong case, but the 2012 prize narrows what is left to credit and the experimental credit is shared among several ion groups. On the chair's question of a second part: with B048 occupying two of three seats, no one-person part is natural, and I would not break up B003 to create one.

uncertainties: Whether the 1e-18 clause and the words lattice clock draw a sufficient line against the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether the clock community would accept that wording.
Whether Katori and Ye alone fairly cover Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the Paris and PTB groups, since my priority details rest on recollection.
Whether B019 would be the better choice in a later year, once the committee has settled how to treat Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the weight of the 2016 prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I work in theoretical condensed-matter and electronic-structure physics, which is adjacent to B019 and B036, and I have no documented personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or any other named candidate. My earlier preference for B019 has no bearing on a recusal question.
